title: The territorial patchwork
hook: An elected monarchy joined many territorial authorities through shared institutions.
notes: Overlay: Reilly/Benedicti, Karte von der Deutschland, Vienna 1796, Rumsey 11151.021. Approximate georeferencing with city/coast controls; retained hand-coloured divisions are the mapmaker’s portrayal, not reconstructed polygons. Credit David Rumsey Map Collection, David Rumsey Map Center, Stanford University Libraries. Adaptation CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Fine print is supplemented by readable modern annotations; a close view deliberately shows only part of the empire. Golden Bull primary text; UNESCO Regensburg. No count of territories or quantified border accuracy is claimed. Source-derived 1789 outline/selected holdings: Alphathon, revision Fenn-O-maniC, CC BY-SA 3.0; full base-map contributor attribution in data/history/hre/attribution.txt. Approximate projection inversion has mean 44 km/max 100 km coastal-control residual, suitable for overview only; historical border accuracy is not established by this fit. The original upload comment and embedded SVG title say 1789 despite a copied Commons summary saying 1279.  Coordinates are approximate named-place locators, not imported surveyed points. Modern borders are hidden. Event cards contain claim-level citations. The later term Holy Roman Empire must not be projected unchanged onto Charlemagne’s Frankish realm.

scenes.title: Election is an institution
scenes.text: The Golden Bull of 1356 specified electors and rules for choosing the King of the Romans. Frankfurt’s meeting role helps explain the empire as a political structure, not simply an emperor’s estate.

scenes.title: A common meeting place
scenes.text: From 1663, the Perpetual Diet sat at Regensburg. A shared assembly operated within an empire whose territorial rulers retained substantial authority.

scenes.title: An imperial outline, circa 1789
scenes.text: The reconstructed map distinguishes imperial membership from possessions held outside the Empire. This source-derived outline is approximate: it describes the mapmaker’s circa-1789 interpretation, with coarse geographic alignment, rather than surveyed legal boundaries.

scenes.title: Dynasties crossed the imperial boundary
scenes.text: The source names Habsburg imperial possessions and Brandenburg separately from those dynasties’ extra-imperial lands. Only the source’s within-empire paths are highlighted. The outer outline supplies context; these are selected holdings, not a complete list of imperial estates.

scenes.title: A dated patchwork
scenes.text: Reilly’s map of Germany, published in Vienna in 1796, preserves a dense pattern of coloured administrative divisions. This archival portrayal provides the territorial fallback: it is a dated map, with approximate alignment, rather than invented modern polygons.

scenes.title: Look closer, keep the context
scenes.text: The Rhine–Main area shows small divisions packed together. Mainz, Trier and Cologne were the Golden Bull’s spiritual electors; Frankfurt hosted elections. The city markers name institutional centres, not the extent of their lands. This 1796 regional view is later than the 1356 rules.
